title: Olympus Edge - p95 streaming readiness and deployment options
summary: Discovery focused on p95 streaming latency targets and concurrency needs for Olympus Edge's real-time assistant. Customer is exploring Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for data residency and cost predictability; they want a pilot to benchmark tokens/sec and end-to-end p95 under realistic traffic shapes.
topics: streaming token/sec benchmarking and tokenization variance
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
security: SOC 2, SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM, audit logs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-01-23 15:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonah Patel (Redwood SE), Ravi Menon (CTO, Olympus Edge), Sophie Alvarez (Infra), Marcus Liu (ML Lead), Tom Hargreaves (Procurement)
Shared: 1) deck: short-redwood-hosted-vs-dedicated.pdf 2) bench sheet placeholder: olympus-bench-templates (link)

Auto-generated summary: Customer building a low-latency streaming assistant for mobile and edge devices; primary KPI p95 end-to-end generation latency <= 150ms for 95% of calls, costs must be predictable; interested in a short pilot across Hosted and Dedicated.

Topics: p95 targets, token/sec, KV cache and prefix caching, burst saturation, fallbacks, security controls (KMS, SSO), pilot steps and metrics.

Action items (auto): Maya to send SOC2 + security doc, Jonah to propose benchmark script, Ravi to confirm sample traffic profile.

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, um this is Maya from Redwood, i'm joined by Jonah, our systems engineer. quick roll call?
[00:00:12] Ravi Menon: hey ravi here, cto at olympus edge, with sophie and marcus and tom.
[00:00:18] Sophie Alvarez: hi all.
[00:00:21] Jonah Patel: hey, nice to meet you all.
[00:00:25] Maya Chen: cool, agenda — we'll do a quick qual baseline, then dig into p95 targets, concurrency shapes, and options (hosted/dedicated/private) and then propose a pilot/bench plan. sound good?
[00:00:36] Marcus Liu: yep sounds good. quick note, we sent a sheet with token distribution and some example prompts, not exhaustive.
[00:00:45] Maya Chen: perfect, we saw that, thanks.
[00:00:50] Ravi Menon: high level — use case is a realtime assistant embedded in our mobile SDK, so streaming is critical. target: users expect snappy responses, we are aiming for p95 generation latency under 150ms end-to-end for typical short prompts (~30-80 tokens).
[00:01:10] Jonah Patel: ok that clarifies things. is the 150ms p95 including network + round trip from mobile -> our backend -> redwood -> response? or just model inference?
[00:01:23] Ravi Menon: good question. needs to be end-to-end from our backend ingress to first token out to our service — we have about 30-40ms on average internal, so model should be in the 80-110ms ballpark to hit 150ms.
[00:01:38] Maya Chen: understood. that sets the bar. what sort of concurrency and burst profile should we assume?
[00:01:45] Sophie Alvarez: steady-state concurrency is low, ~50 concurrent streams, but bursts up to 400-600 during peak campaigns. bursts are short, 2-10 minutes.
[00:01:58] Marcus Liu: also token rates vary, some prompts are short and rely on streaming tokens per sec. for the bench we can provide a mix: 1) short (30 tokens), 2) medium (120 tokens), 3) long (400 tokens) — but long is rare.
[00:02:12] Jonah Patel: good. with bursts like that you'd want predictable capacity. hosted can handle bursts via autoscaling but the tail can be variable; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and more consistent p95s at scale. Private gives you ultimate control but requires ops.
[00:02:28] Maya Chen: quick tradeoff table — Hosted: fastest to launch, good for early testing; Dedicated: predictable throughput, reserved capacity, SLA; Private: VPC/on-prem for strict residency. Also we have prefix/KV caching and continuous batching which can shave p95 by 10-40% depending on prompt similarity.
[00:02:47] Ravi Menon: caching helps a lot for repeated system prompts, yes. question on streaming: do you send partial tokens as they're generated over HTTP/2 or do you push via websockets?
[00:02:58] Jonah Patel: we support streaming over HTTP chunked responses and websockets; for mobile SDK many customers prefer chunked streaming with low-latency flushes. implementation detail: we maintain a KV cache and a streaming pipeline that attempts to flush first-token as soon as the softmax step yields something.
[00:03:16] Sophie Alvarez: is the p95 measured at token emission or at full response completion? we care about the first token and steady token stream after.
[00:03:25] Maya Chen: we can measure both. typical SLOs are p95 time-to-first-token (TTFT) and p95 time-to-last-token (TTLT) for short completions. sounds like TTFT is the higher priority for you.
[00:03:37] Marcus Liu: yes TTFT. also we saw some vendors report p95 per-inference but that hides network latency — we need everything in the loop.
[00:03:47] Tom Hargreaves: procurement note — cost predictability matters. if we go hosted with heavy bursts that spin up more instances, we need guardrails or a cap. how do you do cost controls?
[00:03:58] Jonah Patel: we have quota and burst policies, plus ability to set autoscale thresholds and fallback routes to smaller models or regional variants. Redwood Optimize can recommend batching and quantization settings to reduce token cost while keeping latency SLOs.
[00:04:13] Ravi Menon: curious about tokens/sec rates on streaming. if we get first token at 90ms, what's typical sustained token throughput per GPU for the model size we're considering (we're evaluating an Llama-2-70b variant, quantized)?
[00:04:28] Jonah Patel: rough numbers (very dependent on token length and kv cache hit): for 70b quantized on A100/8000 class equivalence, steady-state token raw throughput can be in the 500-1500 tokens/sec per GPU for sampling with small top-k sampling, but effective end-to-end throughput for many concurrent streaming sessions is lower once you include batching overhead and network per-session costs. for p95 TTFT we focus on kernel-level optimizations.
[00:04:52] Marcus Liu: can you share a benchmark script? we want to replay mobile traces including jitter and small payloads.
[00:05:00] Maya Chen: yes Jonah will share the bench harness. we'll want sample traces and tokenization details.
[00:05:06] [00:10:12] Jonah Patel: (later) one approach: run two pilots — 1) Hosted with a controlled traffic replay to measure TTFT and TTLT and autoscale behavior; 2) Dedicated with a reserved pool sized to your 600 concurrent stream peak to measure p95 tail. we can run a 48-72 hour soak to capture burst patterns.
[00:05:25] Sophie Alvarez: for Dedicated, what's the typical cold-start behavior when scaling up to meet burst? we can't afford >500ms tail during ramp.
[00:05:35] Jonah Patel: Dedicated pools keep GPUs warm; autoscale is faster because you're scaling within reserved capacity. worst-case if reserved GPU usage is exceeded and you rely on burst capacity, there is a ramp that can hit higher tails; we recommend configuring burst capacity plus fallback to smaller variants for non-critical paths.
[00:05:54] Ravi Menon: security — do you support customer-managed KMS, audit logs, SSO and per-route RBAC? we need to satisfy internal audits and a future SOC2 requirement.
[00:06:05] Maya Chen: yes to all. Hosted supports customer-managed KMS integrations, audit logs (retention tiers), SSO/SAML for the Console, and fine-grained RBAC. Private gives you full control with on-prem key material if needed. we'll share the security pack.
[00:06:19] Tom Hargreaves: timeline: we're targeting a live beta in Q2. procurement will need pricing for Pilot and Dedicated ROI.
[00:06:27] Maya Chen: understood. typical pilot structure: 4-6 weeks, two environments (hosted bench + dedicated small pool), success criteria defined as TTFT p95 < 150ms for short prompts and acceptable cost per 1k tokens.
[00:06:40] Marcus Liu: acceptable cost threshold is something we'll provide but ballpark we want predictability under $X per 1k tokens — we'll share later.
[00:06:49] [00:20:01] Sophie Alvarez: network topology question — if we do Private VPC, can you integrate with our Transit Gateway and restrict egress to our managed endpoints?
[00:20:11] Jonah Patel: yes we can support VPC peering/transit gateway setups and restrict egress. private deployments support customer-managed control plane and fine-grained routing.
[00:20:21] Ravi Menon: any gotchas on model quantization? we plan to use int8 or int4. will that affect p95 variance?
[00:20:29] Jonah Patel: quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput but sometimes increases variance in tail latency because dynamic kernel paths differ. our runtime has quantization-friendly execution and we provide recommended profiles per model and workload. Redwood Optimize can suggest the best profile after an initial run.
[00:20:44] Marcus Liu: we want to measure p95 under three conditions: cold cache, warm cache, and live traffic. can the bench script simulate KV cache warm starts?
[00:20:55] Jonah Patel: yes, bench harness can pre-seed the KV/prefix cache so you can measure the delta. we'll script cold vs warm scenarios.
[00:21:03] Maya Chen: let's capture definite next steps and owners.
[00:21:10] Ravi Menon: quick question — competitors, we're talking to Anthropic and evaluating Vertex endpoints as well, and internally some teams want to DIY. just FYI.
[00:21:22] Maya Chen: helpful to know, thanks.
[00:21:27] Jonah Patel: (notes) for the bench we'll need: 1) sample traces, 2) tokenization rules, 3) model binary or reference (if private), 4) target p95 and cost threshold.
[00:21:38] Tom Hargreaves: procurement will want a pilot SOW and an estimate for Dedicated monthly reserved cost.
[00:21:45] Maya Chen: we'll provide a pilot SOW template and a rough cost model within 3 business days.
[00:21:52] [00:30:02] Marcus Liu: one more technical: do you support partial prompt offloading or local KV caching on edge to reduce mid-journey RTTs?
[00:30:12] Jonah Patel: we have prefix/KV caching at the runtime and recommend a hybrid: keep hot prefixes local to your edge when possible and let server-side KV handle shared context. implementing local caches can cut effective TTFT by a measurable amount.
[00:30:26] Sophie Alvarez: and observability — we'll need token-level spikes, trace IDs, per-model breakdown, cost by token.
[00:30:34] Maya Chen: Console gives token-level cost, per-route/model dashboards, and tracing hooks you can wire into your APM.
[00:30:42] Ravi Menon: ok let's recap next steps.
[00:30:46] Maya Chen: recap: Maya to send SOC2/security pack, pricing/pilot SOW, and bench harness template. Jonah to deliver benchmark script and recommended Dedicated sizing for 600 concurrent streams. Olympus to provide sample traces, tokenization notes, and desired cost threshold. we'll target a bench kickoff next week.
[00:31:02] Tom Hargreaves: procurement will also need a draft MSA and terms for pilot.
[00:31:07] Maya Chen: we'll include a pilot-friendly MSA redline.
[00:31:11] Marcus Liu: can we get a short doc listing what metrics you'll collect during the pilot so we can instrument properly?
[00:31:18] Jonah Patel: yes, we'll share a metrics checklist (TTFT p50/p95, TTLT p50/p95, tokens/sec, KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization, queue depth).
[00:31:31] [00:40:00] Sophie Alvarez: any final questions?
[00:40:05] Ravi Menon: none from me. thanks for the clarity.
[00:40:08] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials.
[00:40:12] Jonah Patel: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
